newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs J&J hip implant device.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs J&J hip implant device.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel on Tuesday voted 8-0 to recommend approval of a hip implant component made by Johnson & Johnson's Professional unit.

The committee recommended that as a condition of approval the company provide clearer information on correct device placement and assembly. It also suggested that the firm conduct more tests to determine its true failure rate.
The agency is not bound by the panel's advice, but is expected to follow it.

The Poly-Dial Constrained Liner hip implant device was first sold in 1972, before FDA required effectiveness information on devices. In 1987, it received approval under the 510(k) process -- established in a 1984 law.

In the early 1990s, some devices were reclassified, and the FDA began requiring manufacturers to file a more detailed premarket approval application, including safety and efficacy data. J&J filed in December 1996, and brought the data to the panel on Tuesday.

About 6,000 of the devices have been sold since 1987, with 1,000 being implanted in 1996. It is rarely used, as it is only designed for patients at high risk for hip dislocation, generally due to prior dislocations, joint malformations, or previous failed surgeries.

The company said that 25 years of use has shown that the implant device is safe and effective. Dr. William Wilson of the Seattle Orthopedic & Fracture Clinic presented results of an in-press study. Sixty-one patients, all at high risk for dislocation, received the J&J implant. Only three had later dislocations, an average five months after surgery. There were few complications, which included infections and two cases of a locking ring of the device disengaging.

J&J also said that only 27 reports of serious events had been filed with FDA. Of those, 17 were dislocations. The company said the overall rate of complaints was only 0.68 percent, which it called low.

Panelist Dr. Sally Rudicel of Tufts University, who reviewed the clinical data, said, "The studies do show that there's an indication for this device," and "that it's effective." Rudicel also said that the complications were "not beyond what is expected."
